title: OSHA vs WHS: how do US and Australian workplace safety training duties differ?
description: The US OSH Act relies on a general duty clause plus standard by standard training rules; Australia's model WHS Act builds training into one primary duty.
shortAnswer: The US Occupational Safety and Health Act (OSH Act) places two duties on employers: keep the workplace free from recognized serious hazards, and comply with specific OSHA standards, each of which sets its own training rules. Australia's model Work Health and Safety (WHS) Act instead makes necessary information, training, instruction and supervision part of a single primary duty of care, with a general regulation requiring training to be suitable, adequate and readily understandable.
keyTakeaways: OSHA has no single training rule: training duties sit inside individual standards in Title 29 of the Code of Federal Regulations, each with its own trigger, content, refresher cycle and records.
The model WHS Act puts training inside the primary duty of care at section 19(3)(f), qualified by what is reasonably practicable, and regulation 39 sets a general quality test for all training.
Both systems expect training workers can understand: OSHA through its 2010 Training Standards Policy Statement, WHS through regulation 39.
The WHS Act adds an officer due diligence duty (section 27), which reaches senior leaders personally; the OSH Act places its duties on the employer.
A multinational can run one safety curriculum if it designs to the stricter of the two on each point: OSHA's fixed intervals and records, and WHS's adequacy and verification expectations.

sections.heading: What is the core difference between OSHA and WHS training duties?

blocks.text: The core difference is architecture. The US system is prescriptive and standard specific: training duties are written into dozens of separate rules. The Australian model system is principle based: one general duty to provide necessary training covers every hazard, and specific regulations add detail only for particular high risk activities.

Under [section 5 of the OSH Act](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/oshact/section5-duties), each employer "shall furnish to each of his employees employment and a place of employment which are free from recognized hazards that are causing or are likely to cause death or serious physical harm" and "shall comply with occupational safety and health standards promulgated under this Act." Training requirements come mainly through the second duty. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) publication [Training Requirements in OSHA Standards](https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/osha2254.pdf) collects them, and states that all required training must be provided by and paid for by employers.

Under the model [Work Health and Safety Act 2011](https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2011A00137/latest/text), section 19(3)(f) requires a person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU) to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the provision of any information, training, instruction or supervision necessary to protect all persons from risks arising from work. Training is one way the primary duty of care in section 19(1) is met, not a freestanding obligation. Detail is on [the WHS Act duty to provide training](/regulations/whs-act-duty-to-provide-training).

sections.heading: What does each system expect training to look like?

blocks.text: Both expect training that changes what workers can do, not only attendance. OSHA spells this out standard by standard; WHS sets one adequacy test and leaves the PCBU to show it was met.

OSHA's [2010 Training Standards Policy Statement](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/standardinterpretations/2010-04-28) says that to train or instruct means to present information in a manner employees are capable of understanding. Individual standards then add content lists and timing. The [bloodborne pathogens standard](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1910/subpart-Z/section-1910.1030), for example, requires training at no cost and during working hours, at initial assignment and at least annually, by a knowledgeable trainer, with records of dates, content, trainer qualifications and attendees kept for three years. The full set is on [OSHA training requirements](/regulations/osha-training-requirements).

Regulation 39 of the [model WHS Regulations](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2011L02664/latest/text) requires training to be suitable and adequate having regard to the nature of the work, the risks at the time and the control measures, and readily understandable. Safe Work Australia's [model Code of Practice on managing risks](https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/doc/model-code-practice-how-manage-work-health-and-safety-risks) adds that it is insufficient to hand a worker a procedure and ask them to acknowledge it. That points toward assessment, not sign off.

blocks.title: Practical consequence
blocks.text: Under OSHA, the question an inspector asks is usually whether a named standard's training elements were delivered and recorded. Under WHS, the question is whether the training was adequate for the actual risk and whether the PCBU can show workers understood it. Design evidence for both questions.

The law of the place where work is performed applies. US worksites follow the OSH Act and federal or State Plan standards; Australian worksites follow the model WHS laws in their state or territory, or the Victorian OHS Act in Victoria.

items: **US operations only:** map each task to the OSHA standards that apply, then build training to each standard's content, interval and record rules. The General Duty Clause covers recognized hazards with no specific standard.

**Australian operations only:** identify the risks of each role, decide what training is reasonably practicable to control them, test it against regulation 39, and give officers the information they need to exercise due diligence.

**Both countries:** build one core curriculum by hazard, then add jurisdiction layers. Victoria needs its own references because section 21(2)(e) of its OHS Act carries an equivalent, not identical, duty.
**Other markets:** the EU Framework Directive 89/391/EEC follows a principle based model closer to WHS; see [EU OSH Framework Directive training](/regulations/eu-osh-framework-directive-training).

sections.heading: How can one safety curriculum satisfy both?

blocks.text: Design each hazard module to the stricter rule on every dimension: OSHA's fixed content, intervals and records, and WHS's requirement that training be adequate for the risk and understood. The illustrative mapping below shows one hazard.

blocks.text: The same approach works for every hazard if roles are mapped to tasks first, which is what a [training matrix](/glossary/training-matrix) does. For the competence side, see [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps each hazard, role and control to the OSHA standards and WHS provisions that apply, with provenance to the source text, before content is written. One curriculum can then carry jurisdiction specific requirements as linked obligations, and assessment records show both completion and understanding.

faqs.q: Does the WHS Act set refresher training intervals like OSHA standards do?
faqs.a: Not generally. Section 19(3)(f) and regulation 39 require training that is necessary and adequate for current risks, so refresher timing follows risk, change and evidence of competence. Some specific regulations attach time limits, such as the two year rule for general construction induction when a worker has not done construction work. OSHA standards more often fix intervals directly.

faqs.q: Can OSHA cite an employer for inadequate training when no standard applies?
faqs.a: OSHA's enforcement tool where no specific standard applies is the General Duty Clause in section 5(a)(1), which covers recognized hazards likely to cause death or serious physical harm. Training is not named in that clause, so most training citations arise under the specific standards that contain training requirements.

faqs.q: Do the OSHA Outreach 10 and 30 hour cards satisfy OSHA training requirements?
faqs.a: No. OSHA states that its Outreach Training Program is voluntary, does not meet the training requirements of any OSHA standard and is not a certification. Employers still have to deliver the training that each applicable standard requires.

faqs.q: Who is personally accountable for training under the WHS Act?
faqs.a: The PCBU holds the primary duty, but officers have a personal due diligence duty under section 27, which includes taking reasonable steps to verify that resources and processes for safety are provided and used. Workers also have their own duties under section 28. The OSH Act's section 5 places duties on employers and requires employees to comply with standards.
